s: A code diff is encoded into contextual representations and a pooled semantic vector. Its semantic similarity to another code diff is used for retrieval and for guiding generation.

l: commit message, RACE: Retrieval-Augmented Commit Message Generation, Proposed Approach / Retrieval module .. Generation module
s: A commit message is paired with a code diff in the training corpus and can be retrieved as an exemplar. The generation module produces a commit message token by token using cross-entropy training.

l: large parallel training corpus, RACE: Retrieval-Augmented Commit Message Generation, Proposed Approach / Retrieval module .. Generation module
s: The large parallel training corpus contains paired code diffs and commit messages. The retrieval module searches this corpus for the most semantically similar code diff and its paired commit message.

l: commit message generation dataset, RACE: Retrieval-Augmented Commit Message Generation, Proposed Approach / Retrieval module .. Generation module
s: The commit message generation dataset contains about 0.9 million code diff and commit message pairs. It is used to train the encoder-decoder neural network.

l: neural network-based approaches, RACE: Retrieval-Augmented Commit Message Generation, Proposed Approach / Retrieval module .. Generation module
s: The encoder-decoder neural network is trained on the commit message generation dataset to learn code diff semantics and generate commit messages. Cross-entropy is used as its loss function and AdamW is used for optimization.

l: code diff encoder, RACE: Retrieval-Augmented Commit Message Generation, Proposed Approach / Retrieval module .. Generation module
s: The code diff encoder is trained with a commit message generator to learn semantic representations of code diffs. Its output is mean-pooled into semantic vectors used for cosine-similarity retrieval.

l: Transformer, RACE: Retrieval-Augmented Commit Message Generation, Proposed Approach / Retrieval module .. Generation module
s: Transformer-based encoders are used to capture long-range dependencies and contextual information in code diffs. Their layers include multi-head self-attention, relative position embeddings, feed-forward networks, and add-and-norm operations.

l: decoder, RACE: Retrieval-Augmented Commit Message Generation, Proposed Approach / Retrieval module .. Generation module
s: The Transformer-based decoder generates commit messages step by step from the combined input encoding. It uses masked self-attention, cross-attention, feed-forward networks, and a final MLP with softmax to produce token probabilities.

l: exemplar guider, RACE: Retrieval-Augmented Commit Message Generation, Proposed Approach / Retrieval module .. Generation module
s: The exemplar guider learns a semantic similarity value between the input code diff and the retrieved code diff. It uses this value to weight the input code diff and retrieved commit message representations before decoding.

l: retrieved similar commit message, RACE: Retrieval-Augmented Commit Message Generation, Proposed Approach / Retrieval module .. Generation module
s: The retrieved commit message is treated as an exemplar for generation. Because it may inaccurately describe the input code diff, the exemplar guider controls how much of its information is used.

l: cosine similarity, RACE: Retrieval-Augmented Commit Message Generation, Proposed Approach / Retrieval module .. Generation module
s: Cosine similarity measures the similarity between pooled semantic vectors produced by the code diff encoder. The retrieval module uses it to rank candidate code diffs in the large parallel training corpus.

l: semantic similarity, RACE: Retrieval-Augmented Commit Message Generation, Proposed Approach / Retrieval module .. Generation module
s: Semantic similarity between code diffs is represented through encoder outputs and their mean-pooled vectors. The generation module also learns a similarity value between the input and retrieved code diffs with a sigmoid-based exemplar guider.

l: RACE: Retrieval-Augmented Commit Message Generation, RACE: Retrieval-Augmented Commit Message Generation, Experimental Setup / Dataset .. Evaluation metrics / Baselines
s: This unit describes the experimental setup for evaluating RACE on the MCMD commit-message generation dataset. MCMD contains 450,000 sampled commits for each of Java, C#, C++, Python, and JavaScript, with further filtering for multi-file and unparsable files. Code diffs are converted into token-level change actions, and CodeT5-base initializes the encoders and decoder. Generated commit messages are evaluated with BLEU, Meteor, Rouge-L, and Cider, using multiple neural, information-retrieval, hybrid, and pre-trained baselines.

l: MCMD, RACE: Retrieval-Augmented Commit Message Generation, Experimental Setup / Dataset .. Evaluation metrics / Baselines
s: MCMD is a large-scale dataset containing commits from the top-100 starred GitHub repositories for Java, C#, C++, Python, and JavaScript. It retains 450,000 randomly sampled commits per programming language after filtering redundant and noisy messages, and the study further filters out multi-file commits and files that cannot be parsed.

l: commits, RACE: Retrieval-Augmented Commit Message Generation, Experimental Setup / Dataset .. Evaluation metrics / Baselines
s: The commits in MCMD contain code diffs, commit messages, repository names, timestamps, and other information. The study excludes commits involving multiple files or files that cannot be parsed.

l: code diff, RACE: Retrieval-Augmented Commit Message Generation, Experimental Setup / Dataset .. Evaluation metrics / Baselines
s: The code diff is originally represented at the line level in MCMD. The study converts it into a sequence of token-level change actions and limits its maximum length to 200.

l: commit message, RACE: Retrieval-Augmented Commit Message Generation, Experimental Setup / Dataset .. Evaluation metrics / Baselines
s: Commit messages are used as the generated output and are limited to a maximum length of 50. Their quality is evaluated with BLEU, Meteor, Rouge-L, and Cider.

s: Token-level change actions represent code changes using keep, insert, delete, and replace operations. Each action contains a span of tokens, and replace is extended into replace_old and replace_new to distinguish old and new token spans; difflib is used to extract the action sequence.

s: CodeT5-base supplies the encoder weights used to initialize the code diff encoders and the decoder used in the model. Its original vocabulary is expanded with nine special tokens for the token-level change actions, producing a vocabulary size of 32,109.

l: RACE: Retrieval-Augmented Commit Message Generation, RACE: Retrieval-Augmented Commit Message Generation, Experimental Results / How does RACE perform compared with .. 5.4
s: This unit evaluates RACE against 11 baseline approaches for commit-message generation across Java, C#, C++, Python, and JavaScript using BLEU, Meteor, Rouge-L, and Cider. RACE achieves the best results across all five programming languages and all four metrics, while its exemplar guider improves performance over an ablated version. Experiments show that performance remains generally stable when retrieving between 1 and 9 relevant commits. Applying the framework improves four existing Seq2Seq models, with reported gains ranging from 7% to 73%.

l: RACE, RACE: Retrieval-Augmented Commit Message Generation, Experimental Results / How does RACE perform compared with .. 5.4
s: RACE outperforms all evaluated approaches on Java, C#, C++, Python, and JavaScript across BLEU, Meteor, Rouge-L, and Cider. Its exemplar guider improves results over RACE without the guider, and the framework also improves NMTGen, CommitBERT, CodeT5-small, and CodeT5-base.

s: The baseline approaches include two IR-based approaches, four end-to-end neural models, two hybrid approaches, and three pre-trained-based approaches. RACE performs best among them across all five programming languages and four evaluation metrics.

s: The paper proposes a retrieval-augmented neural commit message generation method that uses a retrieved similar commit message as an exemplar to guide generation. l: The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: This is a sequence of diary records from June through August 1661, centred on Samuel Pepys’s naval, household, family, financial, and social life. Early in June, Pepys works with Sir W. Pen and the Navy Office to inspect and prepare ships at Woolwich and Deptford for an impending voyage. My Lord prepares to go to Algier and Lisbone, entrusting Pepys with preparation work; meanwhile the Office faces an acute lack of money and collapsing credit, with suppliers demanding personal security. Pepys reports these difficulties to the Duke of York, obtains funds and ammunition, and arranges cloth and other provisions for my Lord before seeing him sail from Deptford. Alongside official business, Pepys pursues prospects connected with the Wardrobe, where my Lord suggests he may become Mr. Townsend’s deputy and promises his father first refusal of Mr. Young’s place. He improves his house, oversees painted stairs, buys household goods, begins singing lessons, and frequently visits churches, theatres, taverns, family, and acquaintances. His wife is intermittently unwell, while Pepys takes pleasure in his cleaner home, music, plays including “Bartholomew Fayre,” “The Siege of Rhodes,” and “Claracilla,” and social outings. In July, the death of uncle Robert draws Pepys to Brampton. With his father, he arranges the burial, reads the will, sorts papers, and discovers a less secure and more disordered estate than expected. Copyhold documents are missing, Tom Trice files a caveat for his mother, and Pepys consults relatives, tenants, Sir Robert Bernard, Mr. Moore, Roger Pepys, and others. A later agreement asks Pepys’s aunt to leave the house for £10, but wider claims remain for the law, leaving him worried that debts and disputes will diminish the inheritance. August continues these family and legal concerns while Pepys returns to London work, Privy Seal affairs, and negotiations to add Sir R. Ford’s house to the Office for £200 yearly. He considers Tom’s marriage, worries over his father’s finances and Balty, and notes deaths and mourning in the family. Public and naval anxieties persist: the Office’s bills sell at losses, money is scarce, and strange fatal fevers make the season sickly. Pepys also follows Lord Hinchingbroke’s illness and Lord Sandwich’s fever at Alicante, both of whom improve. The period ends with Pepys conscious of debt, pleasure-seeking, Court disorder, and clerical conduct.

l: Lord Sandwich, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Lord Sandwich is a lord, the diarist’s patron or superior, and Master of Trinity House, with responsibility for Wardrobe business. Before leaving, he places great confidence in the diarist: Mr. Townsend is to explain the Wardrobe administration, and the diarist is to become Townsend’s deputy if Townsend dies. He also proposes that the diarist and Mr. Moore manage the business if necessary, promises the diarist first refusal of Mr. Young’s place if vacant, and entrusts him with a major preparation during his absence. Preparing for a voyage to Algier to settle business and order the fleet, followed by a return to Lisbone with three ships, he obtains ammunition, requires £300 in cloth for presents among the Turks in Barbary, receives the cloth, travels to Deptford, boards a Dutch yacht, and sails after taking leave of the King and friends. While at sea, he falls sick ashore at Alicante, alarming the diarist because of his health and family. Reports say his pain and fever ease; he later writes that he has recovered, remains at Alicante, and expects to proceed toward Portugal, while concern remains over £5,000 intended for his departure.

s: The diarist’s father is a central family and business figure, assisting Samuel Pepys with the cloth business and helping choose scarlet, purple, and black cloth and linen. When a letter reports that Robert is seriously ill and needs help with his business, he prepares to go to him and considers advice about a proposed land purchase. After Robert’s death, he and the diarist work at Brampton through Robert’s will, property, and papers, trying to put the estate in order: letting the crop, arranging for Stankes to manage the business, and discussing the will with the Trices and others. He remains alone at Brampton after the diarist returns to London, while there is concern that he may profit from his London house rather than leave it to Tom. Later he is found well, travels between Brampton and London, and joins the diarist in dealings with Thomas Trice, Dr. Williams, and Mrs. Whately’s household, including examination and proof of the uncle’s will and discussion of a possible marriage for Tom. He notices the diarist drinking, an unfamiliar sight to him. In family matters, he helps confront Pall and agrees she should go into the country with the diarist’s mother. His finances appear precarious: £45 is owed to him, about £45 is owed by him, and this is said to be all his money due in the world.

s: Lord Hinchingbroke, Lady Sandwich’s son, becomes gravely ill and is feared to have smallpox, then steadily improves until sitting up and walking about his chamber.

l: Tom, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Tom, the diarist’s brother and executor, is responsible for their father’s trade. In August 1661 he visits the diarist, hosts family and ladies at dinner, and becomes the subject of marriage discussions, including women of property and the daughters of a broker and Mr. Evans.

l: Lord Crew, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Lord Crew, accompanied by his lady, hosts the narrator warmly, temporarily resides with Sir H. Wright, and advocates naval service as honorable as land war.

l: the Wardrobe, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: The Wardrobe was the subject of my Lord’s instructions to the diarist concerning its management during his absence. My Lord proposed joining the diarist and Mr. Moore in its business if Mr. Townsend died, and promised the diarist first refusal of Mr. Young’s place for his father if it became vacant. The diarist visits the Wardrobe, where he dines with my Lady and is kindly treated. He later brings his wife there to dine, and she is received with considerable attention.

l: Whitehall, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Whitehall is a place repeatedly visited by the diarist and speaker: they seek my Lord, meet Dean Fuller and the Duke of York, and see the Portuguese Embassador take leave of the King. Pepys waits for Lord Roberts at the Privy Seal, then goes with him to his chamber over the gate.

l: the Navy Office, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: The Navy Office is an office that occupies a house under an agreed arrangement. In June–August 1661, the diarist repeatedly attends it for official business while it considers nearby lodgings. Facing a sad lack of money that prevents its men from serving further, it agrees to write to the Duke of York. It also secures Sir R. Ford’s house for its quarters at £200 per year.

l: the voyage, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: The voyage receives imprest funding for my Lord and Mr. Creed, while the diarist and others inspect ships and prepare them to depart.

l: the Wardrobe business, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: is_a mystery [the whole mystery of the Wardrobe] The diarist is promised an important role in the Wardrobe administration: my Lord intends to make him deputy to Mr. Townsend. Townsend is to explain the administration's whole mystery to him.

l: ships, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: On June 1, the diarist, Sir W. Pen, and Mr. Gauden went from ship to ship at Woolwich and Deptford to give orders and assess their readiness to go forth. The diarist and Mr. Creed later sought ammunition at the Tower for my Lord’s ships.

l: Lieutenant Lambert, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: is_a captain [newly appointed] Lieutenant Lambert has been made Captain of the Norwich. He takes the diarist by water to Greenwich, explains various matters concerning ships, and later accompanies him to Mr. Holland's house.

l: Lady Sandwich, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Lady Sandwich is a mother of Lord Hinchingbroke, Sidney, Oliver, John, and a newborn daughter, associated with the Wardrobe and Pepys’s home. Pepys first finds her household merry and well after returning to London. Later, she consults him over Lord Hinchingbroke’s illness and, fearing smallpox, sends her other three sons to his house before fetching them to dine with her. She is also mourning her brother, Mr. Saml. Crew, troubled by toothache, and managing poor housekeeping after my Lord’s departure.

l: the Theatre, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: The Theatre is a house and performance venue. It presents Bartholomew Faire, admired as well acted though excessively profane and abusive, and Claracilla, also well acted. Once thronged, it becomes unusually empty after the Opera begins, ending with the diarist’s first viewing of Claracilla.

l: Bartholomew Faire, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Bartholomew Faire, a theatrical play, is performed at the Theatre; the diarist attends with Lady Batten, Mrs. Rebecca Allen, Mrs. Thompson, and others, praising its acting while finding it profane and abusive.

l: uncle Wight, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Uncle Wight, the narrator's uncle, advises on a Brampton purchase and has daily long fits of stupefaction. After merriment at the Mitre and offense over Brampton, he dines with the narrator and learns of uncle Robert's death.

l: uncle Robert, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Uncle Robert, the diarist’s uncle, suffers serious dizziness and episodic stupidity and speechlessness while his business needs the diarist’s father’s attention. He offers adjoining land for purchase. He dies on the 5th; the diarist goes to Brampton for the funeral and affairs, finding a reasonably supportive will but disappointing estate and papers.

l: uncle Robert's estate, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Uncle Robert's estate proved worth far less than expected; missing copyhold-land surrenders created legal difficulty, leading the family to seek Mr. Philips's advice.

l: the narrator's wife, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: The narrator’s wife, Elizabeth Pepys, is Samuel Pepys’s spouse, active in household, family, and social life. She appears first dressed in a black silk gown laced with black gimp lace, looking very pretty as she walks with him to the Wardrobe and stays with my Lady. Her sore belly becomes serious enough for Dr. Williams to attend her. She travels with Pepys to Whitehall, helps with visits, reports the theft of their silver tankard, and gives him his linen for safekeeping. She visits and travels with relatives and acquaintances, including a Walthamstow visit, trips to Uncle Fenner’s and Aunt Wight’s, the Opera, and the Wardrobe; she also goes with Mr. Hater during his wife’s labour and is expected back from Brampton. Lady Batten and her daughter treat her coldly. Most urgently, she tearfully pleads for help for her brother Balty.

l: fleet, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Fleet is put in order at Algier, then follows the narrator's lord after his three-ship return to Lisbone, meeting him there.

l: my Lord Chancellor, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: My Lord Chancellor begins by directing preparations during the narrator's lord's absence, while facing political opposition from Duke of Buckingham and Lord Bristol.

l: Edward Montagu, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: gives_orders_concerning great preparation [during the narrator's lord's absence] Edward Montagu is to give the narrator orders concerning the great preparation during the narrator's lord's absence.

l: great preparation, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: is_a preparation [for the fleet] The great preparation is to be overseen by the narrator during the narrator's lord's absence, under orders from my Lord Chancellor and Edward Montagu.

l: Huntingdon, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Pepys travels to Huntingdon but finds that the judges have not arrived. He drinks there with Thomas Trice and Mr. Phillips before returning to Brampton.

l: the narrator's house, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Pepys’s house, cleaned after dirt and finished, becomes very clean and neat, greatly pleasing Pepys and pleasing his father on Midsummer-day.

l: Sir George Carteret, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Sir George Carteret is an office member who attends a meeting, helps approve a letter to the Duke of York on financial difficulties, and hosts invited officers for dinner at Deptford, without inviting Pepys.

l: Duke of York, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: The Duke of York receives reports that the office lacks money, supplies, and credit, and meets the speaker and Sir Williams at Whitehall to identify why ships were not sent out. Troubled by the Navy’s financial crisis, he orders a report on the ships and travels on the King’s yacht.

l: money, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: The office lacks money, and its men are not able to serve it more without some money.

l: the office's credit, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: is_brought_low a low level [so that suppliers require personal security] The office's credit has fallen so low that no one will sell it anything without personal security from those involved.

l: Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Samuel Pepys is a person and diarist whose records follow his work, family obligations, finances, household, health, and recreations. He serves in command as an office official at the Navy Office, handling business, letters, naval financial difficulties, sealing matters, and reports to the Duke of York alongside Sir W. Batten and Sir W. Pen. Early on, he arranges cloth for my Lord, accompanies him to Deptford, and later writes to him at sea. He recovers from a severe cold, improves his home with painted stairs, buys a chest of drawers and an Indian gown, keeps linen in his custody, and studies singing with Theodore Goodgroome. A central concern becomes his uncle’s estate: he examines the will, debts, property, surrenders, and papers, seeks advice from relatives and associates, helps prove the will, and fears the proceeds will be less than expected despite an anticipated £200 a year in land. Family anxieties include his parents’ discontent, concern that Tom Pepys may mishandle their father’s trade, arrangements for Pall and Jane, and efforts to protect Lady Sandwich’s younger sons during Lord Hinchingbroke’s illness and possible smallpox. Throughout, he borrows £40 from Sir William Batten, conducts household and legal accounts, and visits friends and family. He frequently attends the Theatre, Opera, plays, and social gatherings, eventually acknowledging that excessive spending and pleasure, especially playgoing, distract him from business and resolving to change. The records end with this self-criticism amid continuing family, household, and office responsibilities.

l: the cloth, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: The cloth, valued at £300 for presents to the Turks in Barbary, is bought for my Lord: two pieces each of scarlet, purple, and black cloth, plus £50 in linen. Mr. Shaw offers the money, my Lord orders Mr. Creed to advance it through Alderman Backwell, and the diarist struggles to send it before it is lately sent to sea.

l: King Charles II, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: King Charles II travels by barge to adjourn Parliament amid pressure over Presbytery and dependence on the Lord Chancellor for policy and service; he later attends Sir William Davenant's Opera and excels at stag hunting.

l: garden stairs, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: is_finished finished [by the painters] The stairs are being painted by the diarist's workmen. The work is finished by the 20th and pleases the diarist greatly.

l: Dutch yacht, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: is_a yacht [Dutch] The Dutch yacht is boarded by my Lord and the narrator at Deptford. It waits while W. Howe brings my Lord's things, then sails from Erith after dinner.

l: the painters, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: paint the stairs The painters work on the diarist's stairs. Their progress causes the diarist some vexation because of delays, but they finish the work by the 20th, to his great content.

l: Brampton, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Brampton is the Pepys family estate, central to managing uncle Robert’s affairs after his death. Samuel Pepys travels there to join his father, remain through the burial and following week, sort papers, inspect lands, handle disputes and relatives, and arrange his aunt’s departure for £10. His father continues settling estate matters there before the mother arrives, while Samuel returns after visits to Yelling and Graveley and ultimately rides toward London.

l: a Margate Hoy, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: is_a vessel [from Margate] A Margate Hoy is hired to carry the cloth and related goods. The diarist sends the things aboard it late at night, hoping they will reach the Downs by the following night.

l: the cloth shipment, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: The cloth shipment is delayed when the purser does not come and the Duke of York has departed, then is sent by a Margate Hoy to the Downs.

l: the diarist's illness, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: The diarist's illness is a painful cold caused by playing in the water. He stays home, keeps warm, breaks wind, and gains relief; by the 19th he reports that he is very well again.

l: the painters' work, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: finishes the stairs [to the diarist's great content] The painters' work on the stairs is delayed and troubles the diarist for much of the 18th and 19th. It is completed on the 20th, leaving him greatly content.

l: aunt (uncle Robert's widow), The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: The narrator found his aunt in bed in a condition he described as extremely dirty and unpleasant. He was repeatedly troubled by what he called her ugly and disagreeable humours during the week at Brampton.

l: Mr. Norbury, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: has_wife Mr. Norbury's wife Mr. Norbury discussed his wife's house and land at Brampton with the narrator over dinner.

l: Mr. Norbury's house and land at Brampton, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Mr. Norbury's wife's house and land at Brampton is too expensive for the narrator to buy, from learning of it onward.

l: Mrs. Frances Butler, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Mrs. Frances Butler, Monsieur L'Impertinent’s sister, is seen by Pepys at Graye’s Inn Walks as his greatest beauty.

l: Pall, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Pall, the diarist’s maidservant, is associated with Kate Joyce at a child’s christening, causes the diarist great trouble, is reprimanded for her conduct and high spirit, and is sent to stay with the diarist’s parents in the country.

l: Pepys's wife's illness, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: has_condition dangerous [as Elizabeth Pepys thinks] Pepys’s wife was unwell, and her sore belly was described as having become dangerous as she thought. Dr. Williams came to see her.

l: the Navy Office, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: The Navy Office is a quiet workplace where Samuel Pepys returns to official business, takes pleasure in authority, and considers Tangier matters and adding Sir R. Ford’s house. With clerks at Tom Whitton’s burial, officials report severe financial losses to the Duke of York. Lack of money leaves the house addition uncertain because of division and rent-guarantee difficulties.

l: Sir Williams both, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Sir Williams both went by coach with the narrator, the narrator’s wife, and Mrs. Margarett Pen to Walthamstow on August 1.

l: the letter from the diarist's aunt, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: The diarist's aunt writes that Robert is seriously unwell with dizziness and needs help with his business, prompting the diarist's father to plan visiting him.

l: Aunt Fenner, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: An aunt known for hypocritical tricks writes that Robert needs the father's help, nears death, and dies.

l: land, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: is_the_subject_of the land-purchase plan [intended acquisition] The diarist is considering buying land that would yield £50 per year. He proposes paying £600 immediately and £150 annually for the remainder.

l: the land-purchase plan, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: A proposed land purchase: the diarist has his father offer £600 immediately and £150 annually until completion, aiming for £50 annual income while appearing able to save more than his actual £500.

l: ships, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Ships' departure is delayed as contrary wind prevents them leaving the river while being made ready.

l: our old club, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Old club members meet the writer at the Bell at the Maypole, talking and drinking with much pleasure.

l: Mr. Chetwind, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Mr. Chetwind, formerly consumptive, becomes fat and sallow through habitual tobacco chewing and praises Hooker’s Ecclesiastical Polity as the best book and the only one that made him a Christian.

l: the Bell at the Maypole in the Strand, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: The Bell at the Maypole in the Strand was the place where the writer met Mr. Chetwind, Gregory, Hartlibb, and Mr. Kipps for drinking and conversation.

l: Hooker's Ecclesiastical Polity, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: A book praised by Mr. Chetwind as the best and the only one that made him a Christian, prompting its purchase.

l: trade of briefs, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: A weekly Sunday trade of briefs becomes a constant practice until the writer and others resolve to give it no more.

l: Portuguese Embassador, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Portuguese Embassador comes to White Hall, takes leave of the King, and arranges the Queen’s overseas departure.

l: Queen, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: The Portuguese Embassador was going to end all with the Queen and send her over. The speaker hoped to make up his expenses by helping prepare things to send with the next fleet to the Queen.

l: order to report on the ships, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: requests an account of the cause of the failure to send out the ships An order had been sent to the speaker and Sir Williams the previous day to give the Duke of York an account of where the fault lay in the ships not being sent out.

l: failure to send out the ships, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: is_caused_by wind against the ships [the stated sole cause] The failure to send out the ships was attributed solely to the wind being against them, which prevented them from leaving the river.

l: Portuguese ambassador's departure and arrangements for the Queen, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: concerns Queen [the ambassador is ending matters with her and sending her overseas] The Portuguese Embassador came to take leave of the King and was going to end all with the Queen and send her over.

l: fleet, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: carries_items_to Queen [the next fleet] The speaker hoped to recover his recent expenses during the summer by helping get things ready to send with the next fleet to the Queen.

l: Roger Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Roger Pepys, a sober man who succeeded Talbot Pepys as Recorder of Cambridge in 1660, welcomes Pepys from Cambridge to Impington, discusses difficulties over an uncle's will, and fears Parliament's profane young men may obstruct serious proposals and cause renewed war.

l: London, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: London is the place Pepys returns to on the 22nd after travel, finding his household and family well. There he resumes household, social, theatrical, official, office, and Privy Seal duties, visits major sites, and continues investigating his uncle’s estate.

l: the Opera, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: The Opera, associated with Sir William Davenant, presents the second part of The Siege of Rhodes and The Witts. It began in late June 1661; on July 2, a delayed performance featured magnificent scenery and generally good acting despite falling dust from a broken board.

l: The Siege of Rhodes, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: The second part of "The Siege of Rhodes" was acted at Sir William Davenant's Opera on July 2nd. The Eunuch performed so poorly that he was hissed off the stage.

l: Claracilla, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: is_a play "Claracilla" was performed at the Theatre on July 4th. The diarist saw it for the first time and thought it well acted.

l: uncle Robert's corpse, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Uncle Robert’s corpse, placed in a coffin on joint-stools in the hall at Brampton, begins to smell and is moved to the yard overnight under watch before burial in church. His will, papers, and estate become central business: money, debts, Sturtlow, and an uncertain inheritance for Samuel Pepys and others.

l: the will, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Uncle Robert’s will is read and reviewed by the narrator, his father, relatives, Dr. John Pepys, Sir Robert Bernard, and Mr. Moore. It gives the narrator little at present, with more after his father’s death, but provides for the family and other kindred. Mr. Moore judges it sufficient despite three witnesses being legatees. Roger Pepys offers guidance and agrees to read the Captain’s will with Pepys’s uncles, while trouble over interpretation and execution is expected.

l: burial of uncle Robert, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: includes funeral sermon [preached by Mr. Turners] Uncle Robert was buried at the church on Sunday after the family prepared ribbons and gloves. Mr. Taylor conducted the burial, and Mr. Turners preached a funeral sermon praising the deceased's widely known honesty.

l: Tom Trice, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: puts_in caveat against the estate [on behalf of his mother] Tom Trice put in a caveat on behalf of his mother, who had received nothing from uncle Robert's will. This development troubled the narrator and his father.

l: caveat against the estate, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: is_on_behalf_of Tom Trice's mother A caveat was entered against the family in behalf of Tom Trice's mother, who was excluded from uncle Robert's will for reasons expressed there. The caveat added to the family's uncertainty about the inheritance.

l: uncle Robert's papers, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: are_in confusion [not well sorted] The narrator's father examined uncle Robert's papers while the narrator worked through them during the week. The papers were badly disorganized, making them difficult to understand and causing the narrator considerable distress.

l: copyhold land, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Uncle Robert’s copyhold land lacks required surrenders, so it passes to the heir at law instead of intended beneficiaries.

l: Cambridge, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Cambridge is a place containing Christ College, King's College chapel, Magdalen, and the University of Cambridge. It is repeatedly a narrator's destination: after preparing to ride there, he arrives, visits colleges, the Rose tavern and university friends, attends Assizes at Castle Hill, dines and drinks, notices university tensions, then rides onward.

l: Impington, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: After leaving Cambridge, the narrator rode to Impington. There he found his elderly uncle Talbot Pepys.

l: Talbot Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Talbot Pepys, the narrator’s old uncle and sixth son of John Pepys, was born in 1583, educated at Trinity Hall, became a barrister and Cambridge official, and died of plague aged eighty-three.

l: Pepys family estate, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Pepys family estate comprises land, crops, copyhold interests, London houses, money, debts, and surrenders. About £500 is found; a house carries a £400 fine and £46 rent. Pepys expects legal claims and debts to reduce £200-yearly land inheritance.

l: Walthamstow, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: is_a place Walthamstow was the destination of the August 1 coach journey, where the narrator and the others visited Mrs. Browne.

l: Samuel Pepys's uncle Thomas, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Dr. Thos. Pepys dined with the narrator on August 2 after the narrator had spent the morning at the office.

l: Parliament, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Parliament begins in disorder, with a delayed expected adjournment and a dispute between its Houses over searches, pamphlets, and seditious books. It faces City of London pressure over the Church settlement, while young men oppose serious men’s measures, raising fears of spoiled affairs and renewed war.

l: will litigation, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Pepys family will dispute remains unresolved: Samuel Pepys, his father, the Trices, Mr. Greene, and others negotiate his aunt leaving the house for £10, while debts, inheritance, and other estate matters proceed to law.

l: Mrs. Margarett Pen, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: comes_from Ireland Mrs. Margarett Pen accompanied the narrator and the others to Walthamstow. It was the first time the narrator had seen her since she came from Ireland.

l: Mrs. Browne, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Mrs. Browne was visited at Walthamstow by the narrator and the others. The narrator gave her six silver spoons for her boy, and the party ate a venison pasty and were merry.

l: the allegation about Lady Batten, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: concerns Lady Batten [alleging that she was such a man's whore] The allegation was that Lady Batten had been a man’s whore. The narrator believed the story was true, but an attempt to reconcile the matter failed.

l: the visit to Walthamstow, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: takes_place_at Walthamstow [by coach] The visit to Walthamstow took place on August 1, with Sir Williams both, the narrator, the narrator’s wife, and Mrs. Margarett Pen traveling by coach to see Mrs. Browne. The party ate a hot venison pasty, were merry, and returned home at night.

l: the journey to Cambridge, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: ends_at Cambridge [on horseback] The narrator prepared for a journey to Cambridge on horseback after Tom came to him on August 2.

l: Quakers, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: continue Quaker movement [in Cambridge and elsewhere] Pepys observes that the Quakers continue to be present in Baldwick and elsewhere, and that they seem to be increasing rather than diminishing.

l: the Privy Seal, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: has_clerks clerks [treated severely by Lord Roberts] The Privy Seal business is delayed because Lord Roberts does not appear during the morning or afternoon of the 8th. On the 9th, Lord Roberts arrives after four o'clock, questions Pepys about his deputation, and then allows the bills to be read and the business to conclude successfully.

l: Lord Privy Seal, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Lord Roberts, the Lord Privy Seal, misses the 8th, delaying Privy Seal business and worrying Pepys over clerks; on the 9th he questions Pepys’s deputation, accepts it, and completes the business.

l: Pepys family business, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Pepys examines his uncle's will, Privy Seal business, and Graveley property obligations while traveling through Brampton, Yelling, and Graveley and consulting relatives and associates.

l: Privy Seal business, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: requires_authorization_from Lord Roberts [as Lord Privy Seal] Pepys is required to attend Lord Roberts at the Seal because it is his month of duty. After delays on the 8th, he and Mr. Moore complete the reading of the bills on the 9th; Mons. Eschar is also waiting there for a warrant for £5,000 for the Earl of Sandwich's preparation for Portugal.

l: Parliamentary conflict, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Roger Pepys describes conflict in Parliament between young men who opposed measures and serious men who advanced them. He also reports that the young men were exceptionally profane and might cause renewed war.

l: Quaker movement, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: is_growing rather than lessening [according to the narrator's observation] Pepys reports that the Quaker movement continues in Baldwick and in every other place he visits. He believes it is growing rather than declining.

l: Lord Sandwich's family, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: depends_on Lord Sandwich [their condition would be endangered by his death] Lord Sandwich’s family is placed under strain by his illness at Alicante. Lady Sandwich sends Sidney, Oliver, and John to Pepys’s house while Lord Hinchingbroke is ill, and Pepys expresses relief that he can provide this service.

l: Alicante, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Alicante is where Lord Sandwich is reported to be sick ashore before his recovery is communicated by letter. Alicante is where Lord Sandwich lay sick with a fever and was twice let blood. He has recovered there but has not yet departed.

l: the smallpox, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: The smallpox is feared to be the cause of Lord Hinchingbroke’s severe illness. Because of this fear, Lady Sandwich sends Sidney, Oliver, and John to stay at Pepys’s house.

l: the fever, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Lord Sandwich is reported to have recovered from his fever. A widespread fever is also said to be affecting people throughout the City and country.

l: Lord Sandwich's illness, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Lord Sandwich’s illness was a serious fever at Alicante, with wind pain in the muscles of his right side, treated by twice being let blood. It caused Pepys to fear for his family’s future, but the pain and fever left him and he recovered, remaining at Alicante while possibly soon returning aboard.

l: Lord Hinchingbroke's illness, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Lord Hinchingbroke’s illness is initially severe, with great fear that it is smallpox. He steadily improves and is described as sitting up and walking about his chamber.

l: the Navy's financial crisis, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: The Navy's financial crisis is caused by lack of money, driving its bills to a 20 percent loss on the Exchange; the troubled Duke of York plans to speak to the King and Council.

l: the sickness in City and country, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: A severe, unusually widespread, strange and fatal fever makes the season sickly everywhere, affecting City and country; it kills Tom Fuller and Dr. Nichols and leaves Lord General Monk dangerously ill.

l: the Court, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: The Court is openly criticized by Ned Pickering for lewdness and beggary and described as corrupt and disordered, with emulation, poverty, drinking, swearing, and loose amours; these conditions prompt fears of ruin and confusion.

l: Sir R. Ford, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Sir R. Ford owns a house that is being considered for addition to the Office.

l: the proposal of marriage, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: A marriage proposal is made by Mrs. Terry for Mrs. Whately’s young daughter to marry the narrator’s brother Tom. The narrator and his father discuss it with Mrs. Terry and the eager Mrs. Whately, who fears her daughter’s youth and small portion but offers £200; they await the father’s response from Hatfield.

l: Jane, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: Jane, the diarist's maidservant for three years, leaves for her mother's country home after receiving wages and an extra 2s. 6d. Though judged lazy and spoilt after Pall's arrival, she is harmless, pleasing, and deeply missed.

l: the clergy, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: has_conduct clerical conduct [criticized as objectionable] The diarist reports that the clergy are regarded as excessively high by many people he meets. He says that people broadly protest against their practice.

l: theatre performances, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: are_a source of expense and pleasure [the diarist feels excessively drawn to them] The diarist sees performances of "The Antipodes" and "The Joviall Crew," finding the former amusing but lacking much else and the latter full of mirth. He also attends a French comedy that he considers poorly performed, dirty, disordered, and unpleasant.

l: Jane's departure to the country, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: is_a departure [Jane goes to her mother] Jane leaves the diarist's service to go to her mother in the country after he settles her wages and gives her an additional 2s. 6d. Her departure causes him considerable sadness because he believes he will not find another maid who pleases him as well.

l: Pall's removal to the country, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: After the diarist rebukes Pall and threatens to keep her no longer, his father agrees that she should go into the country with the diarist's mother and remain there for a time. The diarist views this arrangement as bringing relief from the trouble she causes.

l: the Pepys family estate and finances, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: includes financial debt and borrowing [the diarist is settling the family affairs] The diarist examines his father's accounts and finds that his father is owed only £45 in money and owes about the same sum. He is concerned about what would have happened to his mother if his father had died before his uncle Robert, and he works to settle the family's affairs.

l: court corruption and disorder, The Diary of Samuel Pepys
s: includes drinking, swearing, and loose amours [vices at Court] The diarist sees the Court as afflicted by emulation, poverty, drinking, swearing, and loose amours. He concludes that its condition is likely to produce confusion.

l: clerical conduct, The Diary of Samuel Pepys

l: Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: This document presents Generation-Augmented Retrieval (GAR), a method for open-domain question answering that enriches a question before retrieval. In a retriever-reader system over a large collection such as Wikipedia, GAR trains sequence-to-sequence models to generate three kinds of likely relevant context: answers, answer-containing sentences, and passage titles. These generated contexts, derived from knowledge in pretrained language models and trained with in-domain contexts rather than external supervision or retrieved passages, are appended to the original question. BM25 retrieves passages for the expanded queries, and results from the context types can be fused. GAR is positioned against conventional query expansion, query reformulation, dense retrieval such as DPR, and generative QA. Its focus is retrieval: it extends sparse retrieval beyond the original question while retaining sparse-representation efficiency. The work evaluates retrieval and question answering on Natural Questions and TriviaQA, comparing BM25, DPR, GAR, and RM3-based expansion. It uses Anserini retrieval, BART-large for query-context generation, a BERT-base-initialized extractive reader, a DPR-style span-voting reader, and a BART-large generative reader. Experiments find that generated answer, sentence, and title contexts raise lexical overlap with relevant passages and work complementarily when combined. GAR substantially improves BM25 retrieval, approaches or exceeds DPR at larger retrieval cutoffs, and delivers strong extractive and generative end-to-end QA performance. GAR with BM25 can match or outperform dense retrieval, while fusing GAR with DPR improves results further. The document reports state-of-the-art extractive OpenQA results on Natural Questions and TriviaQA, competitive generative results, and lower training, indexing, and retrieval computation than DPR. It concludes with possible improvements to generation and fusion, joint optimization, hyperparameter tuning, and application to other text-matching tasks.

l: GAR, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: GAR is a generation-augmented retrieval method and query-expansion approach for open-domain question answering. It uses a pre-trained language model and standard seq2seq learning to generate relevant query contexts from a question, including an answer, an answer-containing sentence, and the title of a passage containing the answer. These contexts are treated as retrieval aids rather than necessarily final answers: each is appended to the original question to form generation-augmented queries, retrieval is run separately for diverse contexts, and the results are fused. GAR commonly uses BM25 and sparse representations for Wikipedia passage retrieval, while it can also use or be fused with dense representations such as DPR. Its central value is extracting factual knowledge and relevant contexts stored in PLMs without external resources as supervision, thereby extending sparse retrieval beyond the information in the original question. Generated contexts need only be pertinent for retrieval, not perfect answers. GAR improves BM25 retrieval accuracy on NQ and Trivia, can achieve comparable or better retrieval than DPR at many cutoffs, and sparse GAR is complementary to DPR. With an extractive reader, it achieves state-of-the-art end-to-end OpenQA results, including 41.8 extractive EM on NQ, 62.7 on open-domain Trivia, and 74.8 on hidden Wikipedia Trivia. It also consistently outperforms retrieval methods when the same generative reader is used and is competitive under the generative setup. The method is presented as efficient: training one generation target requires 3–6 hours on one GPU, Wikipedia index construction takes around 30 minutes with 35 CPUs, and it retrieves 1,000 passages for the NQ test set. From generation through augmentation, separate retrieval, and fusion, GAR improves retrieval and QA and can be extended through improved generation, fusion, joint optimization, and other text-matching tasks.

l: OpenQA, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: OpenQA is an open-domain factoid question-answering task that answers questions without a pre-specified domain, commonly using Wikipedia as a large document collection. A typical approach uses a retriever-reader architecture: retrieve relevant documents or passages, then extract or generate an answer. It serves as the evaluation setting for retrieval and reading methods on Natural Questions and TriviaQA. The records present Generation-Augmented Retrieval as an efficient OpenQA approach that uses query-context generation, relevant-passage retrieval, and passage reading; it improves sparse retrieval, reports strong retrieval and end-to-end results, and can be competitive with dense and generative approaches. They also note limits of some reformulation resources and naive pseudo-relevance feedback, and suggest applicability beyond OpenQA.

l: question, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: The question is an OpenQA input expanded before retrieval with generated answers, answer-containing sentences, or passage titles. These heuristically extracted contexts increase lexical overlap with ground-truth passages and avoid externally supervised original-reformulated query pairs, unfolding from augmentation to retrieval efficiency and future extensions.

l: query context, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: A query context is generated from an OpenQA question by pretrained language models without external supervision, as an answer, answer-containing sentence, or relevant passage title. It enriches query semantics and increases overlap with positive passages. Multiple diverse, complementary contexts can be generated and their retrieval results fused to improve accuracy, though hallucinated content may add noise. Future extensions include more contexts, sampling, and testing mutual enhancement among contexts from one generator.

l: BM25, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: BM25 is a classic sparse retrieval method for open-domain question answering. It retrieves passages, including Wikipedia passages, by using a question as a query, and serves as a sparse passage-retrieval baseline implemented with Anserini default parameters. In reader inference it uses 500 passages. It underperforms DPR on NQ retrieval when used alone. Across GAR experiments, BM25 first retrieves with original questions, then with generation-augmented queries; GAR substantially improves it, whereas RM3 yields only marginal or negligible gains. Fusing diverse generated contexts further improves retrieval accuracy, letting GAR with BM25 match or exceed some dense retrieval methods such as DPR.

l: DPR, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: DPR is a state-of-the-art dense passage-retrieval method for open-domain question answering and a comparison baseline. It uses BERT-base for representation learning and generates dense representations for Wikipedia passages. Training with 8 GPUs requires 24 hours, indexing with 8 GPUs 17.3 hours, and retrieval with 1 GPU 30 minutes. DPR is also reused as a retriever in generative QA studies and supplies the reader design and architecture followed by extractive GAR. Across evaluations, DPR generally surpasses unaugmented BM25 at low retrieval cutoffs, but GAR with BM25 can match or exceed it in several settings. GAR and DPR are complementary: combining them consistently improves retrieval and end-to-end QA, though DPR has substantially greater training and indexing computation.

l: retrieval accuracy, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: Generation-Augmented Retrieval improves retrieval accuracy by enriching query semantics with generated relevant contexts.

l: Natural Questions, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: Natural Questions is an OpenQA dataset used as an open-domain question-answering benchmark and in GAR experiments. It has 79,168 training, 8,757 validation, and 3,610 test samples; questions average 12.5 tokens, answers 5.2 tokens, and each question has 1.2 answers on average. It is a main dataset for ablations and evaluation: GAR achieves state-of-the-art extractive performance, improves retrieval and end-to-end results, and gains further EM when combined with DPR, though dense retrieval is stronger at very small cutoffs without DPR.

l: TriviaQA, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: TriviaQA is an OpenQA dataset used in experiments and as an open-domain question-answering benchmark. It has 78,785 training, 8,837 validation, and 11,313 test samples; questions average 20.2 tokens, answers 5.5 tokens, and each question has 13.7 answers on average. GAR is evaluated on it, achieving state-of-the-art extractive performance, 62.7 extractive EM and 62.2 generative EM, with better retrieval than DPR when retrieving at least five passages.

l: extractive OpenQA, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: Generation-Augmented Retrieval achieves state-of-the-art end-to-end performance on extractive OpenQA.

l: extractive reader, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: The extractive reader largely follows the DPR reader design, selects answer spans from retrieved passages, scores relevance and spans, and uses passage-level span voting to aggregate identical-span evidence.

l: Generative GAR, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: Generative GAR is a generative reader for question answering: using BART-large, it concatenates a question with top-10 retrieved passages within 1,024 tokens to generate the desired answer.

l: Wikipedia, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: Wikipedia is a large document collection for OpenQA: its passages and page titles serve as retrieval targets and generation references, then its passages are indexed for experiments, with GAR building an index in about 30 minutes using 35 CPUs.

l: retriever-reader architecture, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: The retriever-reader architecture consists of a retriever and a reader. It first uses a question to retrieve a small document subset from a larger collection, then reads those documents to extract or generate an answer, aiming to improve retriever effectiveness, efficiency, and reader performance.

l: retriever, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: retriever is crucial for open-domain question answering: it selects a small relevant subset of documents or passages when examining a large collection is infeasible. Its accuracy bounds an extractive reader’s performance. In GAR, it receives queries augmented with generated contexts to improve retrieved passage quantity and quality.

l: reader, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: The reader examines retrieved documents or passages to extract or generate an answer; experiments and GAR evaluation use the same reader in extractive and generative forms.

l: sparse representations, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: Sparse retrieval methods use sparse representations and are lightweight, simple, and efficient, but semantic matching suffers when relevant passages lack lexical overlap. Existing OpenQA methods rely solely on question information. GAR enriches queries with information extracted from PLMs before retrieval while retaining exact lexical matching, enabling comparable or better performance than dense representations of original queries. Sparse representations can also be combined with dense representations for better results.

l: dense retrieval methods, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: Dense retrieval methods embed queries and passages in a latent vector space to match semantic similarity beyond lexical overlap, retrieving lexically different relevant passages. They trade this capability for greater computational expense than sparse retrieval and information loss from fixed-size vectors.

l: PLMs, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: PLMs are pre-trained language models that generate contexts for Generation-Augmented Retrieval. Using stored knowledge without external supervision, they provide background and search intent, expand queries, enrich semantics, and support text retrieval or matching.

l: query reformulation, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: Query reformulation research uses text generation for other retrieval tasks, while some methods need task-specific paraphrase data, external resources, or time-consuming reinforcement-learning training. These requirements make them less applicable or efficient for OpenQA.

l: query expansion, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: Query expansion is presented through GAR and pseudo relevance feedback. GAR differs from existing unsupervised methods by generating heuristically discovered contexts from knowledge in PLMs, without external resources or downstream reinforcement-learning feedback. It augments original open-domain question-answering queries for retrieval and is evaluated against the unsupervised RM3 baseline.

l: retrieval, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: GAR is a retrieval method for OpenQA that uses generated relevant contexts from pretrained language models. Evaluated by top-k accuracy against BM25, DPR, and RM3-based query expansion, it improves on BM25 and approaches or exceeds DPR at larger k. Fusing multiple generated contexts helps; future work proposes ranking- and score-based fusion and joint iterative generation-retrieval optimization.

l: dense representations, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: Dense representations of the original queries provide the basis for comparison with Generation-Augmented Retrieval. Combining dense representations with the method's sparse representations produces even better results.

l: generative OpenQA, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: Generative QA uses seq2seq learning to generate answers instead of extracting spans; recent work improves reading while reusing DPR retrieval, while GAR generates pertinent contexts and extracts factual knowledge beyond answers.

l: answer, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: The answer is the default generation target for GAR and is treated as a retrieval context rather than being used directly for closed-book question answering. Even a partially correct or incorrect generated answer may help retrieval if it is relevant to passages containing the correct answer. An answer is one type of query context generated by GAR. Generated answers can be incorrect, but other generated contexts may still contain the correct answer or relevant information.

l: passage, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: Passages are retrieved from the document collection and supplied to the reader. GAR can generate the title of a relevant passage or the sentence in a passage that contains the answer, and it fuses retrieval results from different contexts. A relevant passage is the target of GAR's augmented retrieval process and is later provided to a reader for OpenQA. Generated query contexts increase word overlap between the query and positive passages.

l: generation-augmented query, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: A generation-augmented query appends generated query context to an original question; with multiple contexts, GAR retrieves separately and fuses results.

l: BERT-base, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: initializes reader of DPR BERT-base is used to initialize the extractive GAR reader, which follows the DPR reader setup with largely the same hyperparameters.

l: span, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: A span is a candidate extractive answer within a retrieved passage. GAR computes normalized passage and span scores and aggregates scores for spans with the same surface form across passages through passage-level span voting.

l: BART-large, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: BART-large serves as GAR’s generative reader and query-context generator. It concatenates a question with top-retrieved passages within a 1,024-token limit to generate answers. GAR selects its checkpoint by best validation ROUGE-1 F1, while retrieval accuracy remains relatively stable across checkpoints.

l: retrieval results, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: are_fused equal number of passages [taken from each retrieval source] Retrieval results from separate queries using different generated contexts are fused by taking an equal number of top passages from each source. Weighted fusion and reciprocal rank fusion are also described as possible alternatives.

l: top-k retrieval accuracy, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: Top-k retrieval accuracy is a retriever evaluation metric measuring the proportion of questions whose top-k passages contain an answer span, setting an upper bound on extractive reader answers.

l: Exact Match, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: Exact Match is a reader evaluation metric measuring predicted answer spans that exactly match ground-truth answers after normalization, including article and punctuation removal.

l: RM3, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: is_a unsupervised query expansion method [classic method requiring no external resources] RM3 is used as a classic unsupervised query-expansion baseline, with grid search conducted for its parameters. It is selected because it does not require external resources.

l: passage reading, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: Passage reading is evaluated with Exact Match using both extractive and generative methods. GAR is paired with corresponding readers, including an extractive DPR reader and a generative setup using the question and top-10 retrieved passages. Passage reading is evaluated as the final stage of GAR's OpenQA pipeline. Extractive GAR achieves strong performance on NQ and Trivia, while combining GAR with DPR improves both extractive and generative results.

l: Anserini, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: is_used_for text retrieval [for BM25 and GAR, with default parameters] Anserini is used for text retrieval with BM25 and GAR, using its default parameters.

l: external supervision, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
s: is_bypassed_by Generation-Augmented Retrieval [for forming original-reformulated query pairs] Generation-Augmented Retrieval generates relevant contexts without external supervision. By expanding queries with contexts extracted from pretrained language models instead of reformulating them, it avoids requiring supervised original-reformulated query pairs.

l: RACE: Retrieval-Augmented Commit Message Generation
s: This paper presents RACE (Retrieval-Augmented Commit mEssage generation), a method for automatically generating concise, informative natural-language commit messages from code diffs. Commit messages are important because they document what changed or why, helping developers understand software evolution without inspecting implementation details. Existing neural approaches can generate repetitive or redundant messages, while earlier retrieval and hybrid methods do not fully exploit retrieved commits. RACE retrieves a semantically similar code diff and its paired commit message from a large training corpus. Its retrieval module uses a trained code-diff encoder and cosine similarity. Its generation module encodes the current diff, retrieved diff, and retrieved message; an exemplar guider learns their semantic similarity and weights the retrieved information to reduce the effect of irrelevant exemplars. A Transformer-based decoder then produces the message. The encoder is trained with an encoder-decoder network on about 0.9 million code-diff/message pairs, and CodeT5-base initializes the encoders and decoder. The method is evaluated on MCMD, containing sampled commits in Java, C#, C++, Python, and JavaScript. Diffs are converted to token-level change actions, and performance is measured with BLEU, Meteor, Rouge-L, and Cider against neural, retrieval, hybrid, and pre-trained baselines. Across all five languages and all four metrics, RACE outperforms 11 baseline approaches. Its exemplar guider improves results over an ablated version, performance remains generally stable when retrieving one to nine relevant commits, and the framework improves NMTGen, CommitBERT, CodeT5-small, and CodeT5-base, with reported gains of 7% to 73%. Human evaluation by four experienced volunteers assessed 250 diff-message pairs for informativeness, conciseness, and expressiveness. RACE was reported to outperform NNGen, NMTGen, CommitBERT, and CoRec on all three aspects, with significant improvements; Table 3 specifically gives RACE the highest informativeness and conciseness scores, while CommitBERT has the highest expressiveness score. The paper notes limitations: coverage of only five languages, dependence on a code base, roughly 35 hours of training, and truncation of diffs beyond 512 tokens. The work was supported by the National Key R&D Program of China under grant No. 2017YFA0700800.

l: commit message, RACE: Retrieval-Augmented Commit Message Generation
s: A commit message is a description of a code change’s content or intent, important for software development and maintenance because high-quality messages help developers understand software evolution without inspecting implementation details. It may be empty, insufficiently informative, repetitive, redundant, or difficult to read; in SourceForge projects it can be empty. Messages are paired with code diffs in training data, generated from diffs or reused from similar commits, and limited to 50 tokens. RACE retrieves a similar commit message as an exemplar and uses an exemplar guider to reduce incorrect or irrelevant influence, then generates the message token by token with cross-entropy training. Generated messages are assessed for semantic similarity to code diffs and scored for informativeness, conciseness, and expressiveness, aiming for accurate, readable output.

l: software development and maintenance, RACE: Retrieval-Augmented Commit Message Generation
s: requires time and effort It frequently involves changes to source code.

l: neural network-based approaches, RACE: Retrieval-Augmented Commit Message Generation
s: Neural network-based approaches learn code-diff semantics and translate code diffs into commit messages. They include Seq2Seq, structure- and semantics-aware models, pointer-generator networks, and Transformer-based decoders. An encoder-decoder is trained with cross-entropy and AdamW, though end-to-end neural models generally underperform IR-based approaches across four metrics. Performance differs by programming language, while the proposed framework significantly improves four neural network models.

l: commit message generation, RACE: Retrieval-Augmented Commit Message Generation
s: Commit message generation is an automated software engineering task that creates messages from code diffs, supporting software evolution when developers lack time, motivation, or experience and messages may be empty or difficult to write. It has been approached with rule-based, information-retrieval, neural, Seq2Seq, and hybrid methods. Neural approaches show promising results, while RACE uses retrieved information to improve readability and enhance Seq2Seq models, reporting improvements of 7% to 73%.

l: RACE, RACE: Retrieval-Augmented Commit Message Generation
s: RACE is a retrieval-augmented neural commit message generation method and model. It has a retrieval module and a generation module: first, it retrieves from a large parallel corpus the most semantically similar code diff paired with a commit message, using vector-distance similarity; then it uses that retrieved message as an exemplar to guide generation for the current diff. Its exemplar guider learns similarity between the retrieved and current code diffs, helping use the exemplar without letting retrieved samples dominate generation. RACE supports using k relevant commits and has stable performance across different k values. In experiments run three times with random seeds 0, 1, and 2 and reported as means, it outperforms 11 state-of-the-art approaches and all evaluated baselines on Java, C#, C++, Python, and JavaScript across BLEU, Meteor, Rouge-L, and Cider. The guider improves results over RACE without it. The framework also boosts NMTGen by more than 20% on all programming languages and improves CommitBERT, CodeT5-small, and CodeT5-base. In human evaluation, RACE scores 2.49 (±1.10) for informativeness, 3.08 (±0.96) for conciseness, and 2.85 (±0.84) for expressiveness, exceeding NNGen, NMTGen, CommitBERT, and CoRec on all three measures. It generates concise, readable commit messages with more comprehensive semantics.

l: retrieved similar commit, RACE: Retrieval-Augmented Commit Message Generation
s: A retrieved similar commit serves as an exemplar for generating an accurate message for the current code diff. Because its own message may not match the current diff’s content or intent, RACE uses it only to guide a neural model, avoiding extra or incorrect retrieved information.

l: retrieved similar commit message, RACE: Retrieval-Augmented Commit Message Generation
s: The retrieved similar commit message serves as an exemplar for generating a commit message. Because it may inaccurately describe the input code diff, an exemplar guider controls its influence while guiding the neural network model.

l: code diff, RACE: Retrieval-Augmented Commit Message Generation
s: A code diff is the input to RACE for commit message generation. Originally represented at the line level in MCMD, it is converted into a sequence of token-level change-action spans with a maximum length of 200 tokens. A trained encoder maps it to contextual representations and a pooled vector in a high-dimensional semantic space. That vector is compared, including by cosine similarity, with other code diffs to retrieve a semantically similar commit. The current and retrieved diffs, along with similar commit messages in the generation module, guide generation. Generated messages from randomly selected testing diffs are also used in human-evaluation pairs. When a diff exceeds 512 tokens, it is truncated; this can lose information, particularly for longer diffs with more complex semantics or behaviors.
